questions.problem:
The rate at which the population of yeast cells in a laboratory culture grows $Y(t),$ after $t$ days, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}Y}{\text{d}t}=0.55Y.
$$

How many days does it take for the population to triple? Round your answer to the nearest day.
questions.worked_solution:
We model the population growth using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}Y}{\text{d}t}=0.55Y.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
Y(t)={Y}_{0}\,{e}^{0.55t},
$$

where ${Y}_{0}$ is the initial population.

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the population is triple the initial number. That is,

$$
Y({t}_{1})=3{Y}_{0}.
$$

We solve the above equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Y({t}_{1}) & ={Y}_{0}{e}^{0.55{t}_{1}} \\ 3{Y}_{0} & ={Y}_{0}{e}^{0.55{t}_{1}} \\ 3 & ={e}^{0.55{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.55{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =0.55{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{0.55} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈1.997\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $2$ days for the population to triple.

questions.problem:
The rate at which the price of a particular product changes $P(t),$ after $t$ years, is given by the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=0.042P.
$$

If the price today is $$120,$ how many years will it take for the price to increase to $$750?$
Round your answer to the nearest year.
questions.worked_solution:
We model the price growth using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=0.042P.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.042t},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the initial value.

We're told that the price today is $$120,$ so we have ${P}_{0}=120.$

Therefore, the price $P$ of the product after $t$ years is

$$
P(t)=120\,{e}^{0.042t}\,.
$$

To find how many years it takes for the price to grow to $$750,$ we substitute $P(t)=750$ into the equation above and solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}750 & =120\,{e}^{0.042t} \\ \frac{750}{120} & ={e}^{0.042t} \\ {e}^{0.042t} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.042t}) & =ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ 0.042t & =ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ t & =\frac{1}{0.042}ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ t & ≈43.633\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $44$ years for the price to increase to $$750.$

questions.problem:
A balloon is being deflated. The rate at which the diameter of the balloon decays $D(t),$ after $t$ seconds, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=-0.20D.
$$

How long does it take for the balloon’s diameter to reduce to $15%$ of its original diameter?  Round your answer to the nearest second.
questions.worked_solution:
We model the diameter of the balloon using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=-0.20D.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
D(t)={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.20t},
$$

where ${D}_{0}$ is the initial diameter.

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the diameter of the balloon is $15%$ of its original diameter. That is,

$$
D({t}_{1})=0.15{D}_{0}.
$$

We solve the above equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.15{D}_{0} & ={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.20{t}_{1}} \\ 0.15 & ={e}^{-0.20{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.15) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-0.20{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.15) & =-0.20{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.15)}{0.20} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈9.486\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}R}{\text{d}t}=-0.25R.
$$

If there are $20\,000$ unprocessed records at the start of the scan, how many minutes does it take for the number of unprocessed records to decrease to $1\,000?$ Round your answer to the nearest minute.
questions.worked_solution:
We model the number of unprocessed records using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}R}{\text{d}t}=-0.25R.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
R(t)={R}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.25t},
$$

where ${R}_{0}$ is the initial number of unprocessed records.

We're told that there are $20\,000$ unprocessed records at the start of the scan, so we have ${R}_{0}=20\,000.$

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the number of unprocessed records has decreased to $1\,000.$ That is,

$$
R({t}_{1})=1\,000.
$$

We solve the above equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,000 & =20\,000{e}^{-0.25{t}_{1}} \\ \frac{1\,000}{20\,000} & ={e}^{-0.25{t}_{1}} \\ 0.05 & ={e}^{-0.25{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.05) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-0.25{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.05) & =-0.25{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.05)}{-0.25} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈11.982\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $12$ minutes for the number of unprocessed records to decrease to $1\,000.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing an Unknown Time Given an Exponential Growth or Decay Model With an Unknown Rate
questions.problem: A car is traveling along a straight road to a particular destination. The remaining distance $D(t)$ varies according to the differential equation ${D}^{′}(t)=-rD(t),$ where $t$ is the time, measured in hours, and $r>0.$ Two hours into the journey, the remaining distance is three-quarters of the journey's total distance. How long does it take for the remaining distance to reduce to one-third of the journey's total distance? Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
D(t)={D}_{0}{e}^{-rt},
$$

where ${D}_{0}$ is the distance when $t=0.$

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the distance equals $\frac{1}{3}{D}_{0}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}D({t}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{3}{D}_{0}\,⇒\,{D}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}}=\frac{1}{3}{D}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{3}{D}_{0} \\ \cancel{{D}_{0}}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{3}\cancel{{D}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ -r{t}_{1} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that two hours into the journey, the remaining distance is three-quarters of the journey's total distance. Therefore,

$$
D(2)=\frac{3}{4}{D}_{0}\,⇒\,{D}_{0}{e}^{-2r}=\frac{3}{4}{D}_{0}.
$$

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{0}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{3}{4}{D}_{0} \\ \cancel{{D}_{0}}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{3}{4}\cancel{{D}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-2r} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-2r}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) \\ -2r & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75) \\ r & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this into $(∗)$ and evaluating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{r} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75)}{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75)} \\  & ≈7.6,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: The number of subscribers $N(t)$ to an e-learning platform varies according to the differential equation ${N}^{′}(t)=rN(t),$ where $t$ is the time since the platform was launched, measured in weeks, and $r>0.$ It is known that the number of subscribers doubles after the first four weeks. How long does it take for the number of subscribers to triple after the platform is launched? Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
N(t)={N}_{0}{e}^{rt},
$$

where ${N}_{0}$ is the number of subscribers when $t=0.$

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the number of subscribers equals $3{N}_{0}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}N({t}_{1}) & =3{N}_{0}\,⇒\,{N}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}}=3{N}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =3{N}_{0} \\ \cancel{{N}_{0}}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =3\cancel{{N}_{0}} \\ {e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ r{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that the number of subscribers doubles after the first four weeks the platform is launched. Therefore,

$$
N(4)=2{N}_{0}\,⇒\,{N}_{0}{e}^{4r}=2{N}_{0}.
$$

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{N}_{0}{e}^{4r} & =2{N}_{0} \\ \cancel{{N}_{0}}{e}^{4r} & =2\cancel{{N}_{0}} \\ {e}^{4r} & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{4r}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ r & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this into $(∗)$ and evaluating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{r} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{4})} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & ≈6.3,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}{e}^{rt},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the mouse population when $t=0.$

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the mouse population equals $8{P}_{0}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P({t}_{1}) & =8{P}_{0}\,⇒\,{P}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}}=8{P}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =8{P}_{0} \\ \cancel{{P}_{0}}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =8\cancel{{P}_{0}} \\ {e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =8 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ r{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P(2)=5{P}_{0}\,⇒\,{P}_{0}{e}^{2r}=5{P}_{0}.

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$

rounded to one decimal place.

where ${V}_{0}$ is the value when $t=0.$

$$

$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that the value reduces by one-half after the first year. Therefore,

$$
V(1)=\frac{1}{2}{V}_{0}\,⇒\,{V}_{0}{e}^{-r}=\frac{1}{2}{V}_{0}.

questions.problem: The price $P(t)$ of a particular good varies according to the differential equation ${P}^{′}(t)=rP(t),$ where $t$ is the time, measured in years, and $r>0.$ It is known that the price of the good tripled after the first six years. How long did it take for the price to double from the initial price?
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}{e}^{rt},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the price of the good when $t=0.$

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the price equals $2{P}_{0}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P({t}_{1}) & =2{P}_{0}\,⇒\,{P}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}}=2{P}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{0}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =2{P}_{0} \\ \cancel{{P}_{0}}{e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =2\cancel{{P}_{0}} \\ {e}^{r{t}_{1}} & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ r{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that the price of the good tripled after the first six years. Therefore,

$$
P(6)=3{P}_{0}\,⇒\,{P}_{0}{e}^{6r}=3{P}_{0}.
$$

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{0}{e}^{6r} & =3{P}_{0} \\ \cancel{{P}_{0}}{e}^{6r} & =3\cancel{{P}_{0}} \\ {e}^{6r} & =3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6r}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ r & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this into $(∗)$ and evaluating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{r} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{6})} \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & ≈3.8,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: The population $P(t)$ of rabbits in a forest after $t$ weeks can be modeled by the differential equation ${P}^{′}(t)=0.11P(t).$ If there were $786$ rabbits after $8$ weeks, calculate the rabbit population after $15$ weeks.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.11t},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the initial number of rabbits.

We are given that after $8$ weeks, there were $786$ rabbits. So, substituting $t=8$ and $P(8)=786$ into our general solution and solving for ${P}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(8) & ={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.11\cdot 8} \\ 786 & ={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.88} \\ {P}_{0} & =\frac{786}{{e}^{0.88}} \\  & ≈326.019,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Hence, our particular solution is

$$
P(t)=326.019\,{e}^{0.11t}.
$$

We want to find the number of rabbits after $15$ weeks. So, substituting $t=15$ into our particular solution, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(15) & =326.019\,{e}^{0.11\cdot 15} \\  & =326.019\,{e}^{1.65} \\  & ≈1\,698,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest whole number. 

Therefore, there will be about $1\,698$ rabbits after $15$ weeks.

canonical_examples.problem:
The rate at which the balance in a savings account grows $B(t),$ after $t$ years, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d B}{\textrm d t} = 0.05B.
$$

How many years does it take for the balance to increase by $60\%?$  Round your answer to the nearest year.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We model the balance growth using the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d B}{\textrm d t} = 0.05B.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
B(t) = B_0\,e^{0.05t},
$$

where $B_0$ is the initial balance.

Let $t_1$ be the time when the balance has increased by $60\%.$ That is,

$$
B(t_1) = 1.6B_0.
$$

We solve the above equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B({t}_{1}) & ={B}_{0}{e}^{0.05\cdot {t}_{1}} \\ 1.6{B}_{0} & ={B}_{0}{e}^{0.05{t}_{1}} \\ 1.6 & ={e}^{0.05{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.05{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6) & =0.05{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6)}{0.05} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈9.40\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $9$ years for the balance to increase by $60\%.$

canonical_examples.problem:
The rate at which the amount of medicine in a person’s bloodstream decreases $M(t),$ after $t$ hours, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}M}{\textrm{d}t} = -0.08M.
$$

How many hours does it take for the amount of medicine to decrease to $30\%$ of the original amount?  Round your answer to the nearest hour.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We model the amount of medicine using the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}M}{\textrm{d}t} = -0.08M.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0\,e^{-0.08t},
$$

where $M_0$ is the initial amount of medicine.

Let $t_1$ be the time when the amount of medicine is $30\%$ of the original amount. That is,

$$
M(t_1) = 0.30M_0.
$$

We solve the above equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.30{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}} \\ 0.30 & ={e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30) & =-0.08{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30)}{0.08} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈15.050\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $15$ hours for the amount of medicine to decrease to $30\%$ of the original amount.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing an Unknown Time Given an Exponential Growth or Decay Model With an Unknown Rate
canonical_examples.problem: During an experiment, the weight $W(t)$ of an object varies according to the differential equation $W'(t) = -r W(t),$ where $t$ is the time, measured in hours, and $r > 0.$ It is known that the object's weight reduces by three-quarters after the first two hours. How long does it take for the object's weight to reduce to one-sixth of its original weight? Round your answer to one decimal place.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
W(t) = W_0 e^{-rt},
$$

where $W_0$ is the weight when $t=0.$

Let $t_1$ be the time when the weight equals $\dfrac{1}{6}W_0.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}W({t}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0}\,⇒\,{W}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}}=\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0} \\ \cancel{{W}_{0}}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6}\cancel{{W}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{6}) \\ -r{t}_{1} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that the weight reduces by three-quarters after the first two hours. Therefore, one-quarter of the weight remains, and we have

$$
W(2) = \dfrac{1}{4}W_0\quad \Rightarrow\quad W_0e^{-2r} = \dfrac{1}{4}W_0
$$

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{0}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4}{W}_{0} \\ \cancel{{W}_{0}}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4}\cancel{{W}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-2r}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}) \\ -2r & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ r & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{4}^{1/2} \\ r & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this into $(*)$ and evaluating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{r} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & ≈2.6\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place. 

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $2.6$ hours for the weight to reduce to one-sixth of its original weight.

canonical_examples.problem: A marathon runner is participating in a race. The remaining distance $D(t)$ they have left to run $t$ hours since starting the race can be modeled by the differential equation $D'(t)= -0.8D(t).$ Two hours into the race, they have $6\,\text{km}$ remaining. Calculate the distance remaining after four hours.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
D(t) = D_0\,e^{-0.8t},
$$

where $D_0$ is the remaining distance when $t=0.$

We are given that the remaining distance was $6\,\text{km}$ after $2$ hours. So, substituting $t=2$ and $D(2)=6$ into our general solution and solving for $D_0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D(2) & ={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.8\cdot 2} \\ 6 & ={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-1.6} \\ {D}_{0} & =\frac{6}{{e}^{-1.6}} \\  & ≈29.718,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Hence, our particular solution is

$$
D(t) = 29.718\,e^{-0.8t}.
$$

We want to find the distance remaining after $4$ hours. So, substituting $t=4$ into our particular solution, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D(4) & =29.718\,{e}^{-0.8\cdot 4} \\  & =29.718\,{e}^{-3.2} \\  & ≈1.2,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Therefore, the remaining distance after $4$ hours is $1.2\,\text{km}.$
